L128: ABSTRACT
L129: 
L130: When extracted and analysed in tandem, proteomics and lipid residue analysis can provide high resolution
L131: 
L132: identication of ancient foodstuff. Here, we apply lipid residue and shotgun proteomic analyses to 11 ceramic
L133: vessel sherds from the Gujarat, India-based Indus Valley Civilization site of Kotada Bhadli. Our results demon-
L134: 
L135: strate variable success. Lipids were successfully recovered from each ceramic vessel and suggest the presence of
L136: 
L137: dairy and meat from cattle/buffalo, and meat from sheep/goat and monogastric animals, such as pigs and birds.
L138: 
L139: Additionally, we were also able to identify the presence of plant products such as leafy vegetables, oils and
L140: broomcorn millets. In contrast, none of the extracted proteins could be condently traced to specic foods or
L141: 
L142: ingredients and were thus unable to contribute to broader interpretations of foodways at Kotada Bhadli.
L143: 
L144: Nevertheless, our results present an opportunity to discuss pathways for improving proteomic methods, and
L145: 
L146: advocate for the need to report negative results as well as positive ones. We support continued efforts to apply
L147: multi-proxy approaches to the study of ancient ceramics and consider future applications of shotgun proteomics
L148: 
L149: in this rapidly evolving eld.

L151: 1. Introduction
L152: 
L153: Food is essential to human life, and archaeologists have long been
L154: 
L155: interested in reconstructing ancient foodways to understand how food
L156: 
L157: was acquired, processed, prepared, consumed, and discarded. Re-
L158: 
L159: constructions of ancient foodways can provide vital information on
L160: 
L161: technology, environmental interactions, socio-economic practices, rit-
L162: uals, and religious identities. While ancient diet and cuisine have always
L163: 
L164: intrigued archaeologists, formal research on the reconstruction of
L165: 
L166: ancient foodways began with the introduction of “New” or Processual
L167: 
L168: archaeology in the later part of the 20th century (e.g. Watson 2009).
L169: 
L170: Archaeologists interested in reconstructing past subsistence practices
L171: 
L172: primarily rely on macro remains of plants and animals that are preserved
L173: 
L174: in the archaeological record. In recent years, however, owing to the
L175: advancement and availability of scientic techniques, archaeologists are
L176: 
L177: now able to incorporate various proxies, such as micro botanical
L178: 
L179: remains (starch and phytoliths), isotopes, and molecular remains such as
L180: 
L181: lipids, proteins, and DNA, to reconstruct ancient foodways (Bates et al.,
L182: 
L183: 2017; Chakraborty et al., 2018, 2020; Charters et al., 1993; Colonese
L184: 
L185: et al., 2017; Evershed, 1993 ; García-Granero et al., 2014, 2022; Hendy
L186: 
L187: et al., 2018; Heron et al., 1993; Kashyap, 2010; Nowell et al., 2016;
L188: Pavelka et al., 2016; Sawafuji et al., 2020; Suryanarayan et al., 2021).
L189: 
L190: One such method – the reconstruction of foodways from food residues
L191: 
L192: absorbed and adherent in unglazed pottery vessels – has gained
L193: 
L194: considerable popularity. Fatty acids extracted from these residues have
L195: 
L196: demonstrated signicant potential in informing foodways due to their
L197: 
L198: hydrophobic nature and stability in extreme burial environments. The
L199: 
L200: application of lipid residue analysis within variable geographic contexts
L201: has contributed valuable information on the processing and utilization
L202: 
L203: of various food items that are generally not preserved in the archaeo-
L204: 
L205: logical record, such as dairy, wine, tars, resins, oils, and fats. While
L206: 
L207: South Asia was late in contributing to lipid residue analysis research, a

L237: Despite its widespread success, a major limitation of the lipid residue
L238: 
L239: analysis technique is its inability to provide more specic taxonomic

L241: identication for food items (Whelton et al., 2021). This method is also
L242: less successful at detecting food items with low lipid content, such as
L243: 
L244: grains and vegetables (Irto et al., 2022). The establishment of lipid
L245: 
L246: biomarkers can be used to identify specic food items from plants, such
L247: 
L248: as millets, maize, cereal grains, grapes and occasionally resins, and an-
L249: 
L250: imal products such as aquatic fats, adipose tissue and dairy fats
L251: 
L252: (Colonese et al., 2017; Copley et al., 2005; Craig et al., 2007; Hammann
L253: 
L254: and Cramp, 2018; Murakami et al., 2022; Pfeiffer et al., 2016; Reber
L255: et al., 2004; Tach´

L258: 
L259: markers do not often preserve in the archaeological record, and when
L260: 
L261: present, must be carefully interpreted (Whelton et al., 2021). Ad-
L262: 
L263: vancements in the 1990’s compound-specic carbon isotope analysis
L264: 
L265: (CSIA) of fatty acids have made it possible to identify meat from rumi-
L266: 
L267: nant and non-ruminant animals, dairy, and aquatic fats, etc.
L268: 
L269: (Chakraborty et al., 2020; Dudd and Evershed, 1998; Evershed et al.,
L270: 1997; Evershed et al., 1994, 2002; Mukherjee et al., 2007; Reber et al.,
L271: 
L272: 2004; Webb et al., 2018). Further studies have, however, highlighted the
L273: 
L274: complexities of applying CSIA in cases of mixed ingredients. For
L275: 
L276: example, the mixing between plant and animal fats, as well as between
L277: 
L278: different animal fats, can alter isotopic values, resulting in false identi-
L279: 
L280: cations of meat and dairy (Fernandes et al., 2018; Hendy et al., 2018).
L281: 
L282: The mixing of different food items and its impact on CSIA is particularly
L283: concerning because archaeology ceramic vessels may have been used for
L284: 
L285: a long period of time before discard and were most likely used to process
L286: 
L287: and consume more than one type of food item. Experimental studies
L288: 
L289: have shown that the absorbed residue extracted from pottery is a
L290: 
L291: mixture of ingredients cooked during the vessel’s use life (Miller et al.,
L292: 
L293: 2020); however, not all pottery will exhibit mixed residues and certain
L294: 
L295: types of pottery could have been used to process or contain very specic
L296: food items that were never mixed, as seen in ethnographic examples of
L297: 
L298: yogurt or other dairy processing containers, for example.
L299: 
L300: Due to these limitations of lipid residue analysis, studies have
L301: 
L302: recently begun applying multi-proxied approaches to the analysis of
L303: 
L304: pottery residues, often combining lipid residue analysis with techniques
L305: 
L306: such as archaeozoological remains (Mukherjee et al., 2007), stable
L307: 
L308: carbon isotopes from animal dentition (Chakraborty, 2019; Chakraborty
L309: et al., 2020), microbotanical analysis (phytoliths and starch grain
L310: 
L311: identication) and shotgun proteomics for more informed in-
L312: 
L313: terpretations of organic residue composition (Evans et al., 2023; Gar-
L314: 
L315: cía-Granero et al., 2022; Hendy et al., 2018; Lyu et al., 2024). In this
L316: 
L317: study, we have combined methods for analysis of lipids and proteins to
L318: 
L319: investigate absorbed residues from ceramic sherds from Kotada Bhadli,
L320: 
L321: an Indus Valley site.
L322: 
L323: Shotgun proteomics is a bottom-up approach for ancient protein
L324: analysis which allows for the identication and characterization of all
L325: 
L326: proteins within a substrate (Hendy et al., 2018; Warinner et al., 2022).
L327: 
L328: Shotgun proteomics can identify individual food components of complex
L329: 
L330: mixtures, and differentiate proteins by taxa (plants, animals, and mi-
L331: 
L332: crobes) and by tissue (e.g. leaf/stem, and milk/meat) (Solazzo et al.,
L333: 
L334: 2008a, 2008b; Shevchenko et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2014; Hendy et al.,
L335: 
L336: 2018; Evans et al., 2023). Proteins may also provide insights into past
L337: food preparation, as transformative practices such as boiling or
L338: 
L339: fermentation affect the overall protein composition of foodstuff (Barker
L340: 
L341: et al., 2012; 2018; Paskulin et al., 2024). Thus, protein analysis has a
L342: 
L343: signicant potential to contribute to studies of foodways through the
L344: 
L345: identication of mixed foodstuff specic to tissue and, to a degree, to
L346: 
L347: taxa.
L348: 
L349: Outside of cases of exceptional preservation (see Solazzo et al.,
L350: 
L351: 2008a, 2008b; Shevchenko et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2014), successful
L352: palaeoproteomic applications have determined that proteins preserve
L353: 
L354: best when encased within mineral substrates (e.g., bone, enamel,
L355: 
L356: eggshell, mollusc shell) where proteins can survive for thousands and
L357: 
L358: potentially millions of years (Cappellini et al., 2012, 2019; Demarchi
L359: 
L360: et al., 2016; Welker et al., 2019; Sakalauskaite et al., 2020). The ceramic
L361: 
L362: matrix, being an anthropogenic mineral-construct, thus has potential for
L363: 
L364: binding and preserving proteins. Experimental studies testing the ca-
L365: pacity of proteins to bind to ceramic matrices, however, have had var-
L366: 
L367: iable results. Barker et al. (2012), for example, conclude that while
L368: 
L369: proteins do bind to ceramics, the mechanisms of binding are poorly
L370: 
L371: understood. Furthermore, Barker et al. (2018) suggest that chemical
L372: 
L373: processes such as hydrolysis are likely to damage bonds formed between
L374: 
L375: ceramic and protein during food preparation, even within the rst 6
L376: 
L377: months of burial. Likewise, Evans et al. (2024) found that a range of
L378: variables can affect ancient protein preservation – including the original
L379: 
L380: mixture of ingredients – and that proteins are more likely to survive
L381: 
L382: within residues (e.g. foodcrust) than in the ceramic matrix itself.
L383: 
L384: Variable success in the application of proteomics to ceramics has
L385: 
L386: further complicated our understanding of protein binding and preser-
L387: 
L388: vation. Hendy et al. (2018) successfully recovered proteins preserved in
L389: 
L390: residues and ceramic matrix from 9 of the 10 analysed ceramics sherds
L391: from Catalhoyuk, identifying evidence for dairy, cereal grains, legumes,
L392: 
L393: and non-dairy animal products. Nonetheless, the high success rate
L394: 
L395: exhibited in the Catalhoyuk study has been difcult to replicate. For
L396: 
L397: example, only one of the eight sherds analysed by Chowdhury et al.
L398: 
L399: (2022) yielded viable archaeological proteins, providing limited early
L400: 
L401: evidence (mid-2nd millennium BCE) for soybean use in Tell Khaiber,
L402: 
L403: southern Iraq. Evans et al. (2023) identied dairy proteins in milk-scale
L404: deposits from four sherds of Late Neolithic pottery in Poland, providing
L405: 
L406: complementary information to lipid residue analysis conducted in tan-
L407: 
L408: dem, despite the low sample size. Eight of the nine ceramic sherds from
L409: 
L410: Ba ħ rija (Malta) analysed by Tanasi et al. (2021) yielded archaeological
L411: 
L412: proteins, primarily originating from wheat and dairy products. In gen-
L413: 
L414: eral, however, applications of shotgun proteomics to archaeological
L415: 
L416: ceramics are often characterized by low sample sizes and low success
L417: rates. While low sample sizes are often due to cost restraints, low success
L418: 
L419: rates reect a multitude of complex challenges facing the advancement
L420: 
L421: of palaeoproteomics, many of which are outlined in Hendy et al. (2018)
L422: 
L423: and Warinner et al. (2022). Protein detection, identication, and
L424: 
L425: authentication represent three of the most signicant challenges and are
L426: 
L427: typically addressed on a case-by-case, and even sample-to-sample, basis
L428: 
L429: (Schroeter and Cleland, 2016; Cleland and Schroeter, 2018; Hendy et al.,
L430: 2018; Rams ø e et al., 2021; Tanasi et al., 2021; Warinner et al., 2022;
L431: 
L432: Rodriguez Palomo et al., 2023; Evans et al., 2024). Experimental tests of
L433: 
L434: sampling, extraction, and analytical methods are important in
L435: 
L436: advancing the method, but practical applications areessential due to the
L437: 
L438: unique set of restraints ancient samples place upon modern methods.

L440: Here, we apply proteomics to ceramic sherds from the Indus Valley
L441: 
L442: Civilization site of Kotada Bhadli, representing the rst application of

L444: 
L445: using both lipid residue analysis and palaeoproteomics for the robust
L446: 
L447: identication of food items and a more informed reconstruction of in-
L448: 
L449: gredients cooked and stored in the ceramic vessels.
